entities.summary:
Martín de Azpilcueta (1492–1586), known as Doctor Navarrus, was a towering figure in Navarrese jurisprudence, theology, and nascent economic thought, whose intellectual contributions spanned the late Renaissance and early modern periods. Born in Barásoain, Kingdom of Navarre, he became a central luminary of the School of Salamanca, a group renowned for its pioneering work in economics, law, and moral theology. Azpilcueta's significance lies in his rigorous application of scholastic methodology to contemporary challenges, particularly concerning monetary theory and ethical finance, making him a crucial bridge between medieval scholasticism and modern economic analysis.

Azpilcueta’s academic career saw him teaching canon law at the Universities of Toulouse, Cahors, Salamanca, and Coimbra, where his lectures attracted vast audiences and earned him widespread renown. His most celebrated work, the *Manual de confesores y penitentes* (Handbook for Confessors and Penitents, 1556), systematically addressed complex moral and legal dilemmas, including pioneering discussions on the quantity theory of money. In it, he famously articulated that 'all merchandise becomes dearer when it is in great demand and short supply... and money, no less than other merchandise, has a price which can vary,' observing the inflationary effects of New World silver influx into Spain. He also served as a respected confessor and advisor to powerful figures, including King Philip II of Spain and Pope Gregory XIII in Rome, influencing papal reforms and legal decisions.
